articleTitle: Gate arrays using the Falcon multiproject wafer service
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: Over the last few years custom and semi-custom integrated circuits have become a common, and accepted, interconnect technology-both in the commercial and educational sectors. It is now common practice for ASICs to be routinely considered in new equipment, and new graduates are increasingly being expected to have a knowledge of the design route to silicon with a good familiarity of the design tools likely to be encountered in industry. This greater awareness of the uses and advantages of this technology has generated greater demands from silicon suppliers-both in terms of the product range available and the services offered. Micro Circuit Engineering in Tewkesbury have been involved in the supply of custom silicon for over 15 years, and this paper is intended to review the experience we have gained in this time, and to highlight the trends we are observing, and the way we are responding to these demands, by looking at some of the designs in which we have been involved.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Innovative mixed mode simulation and silicon compilation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: The Solo development systems now enables an engineer with no IC design experience to compile a highly complex design at a high level-and include all his system requirements, from OP AMP to a core micro. Out of 400 designs already through this route none have failed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The benefits of built in self test for OEM designers
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: An important advantage of full speed Autonomous Built In Self Test over conventional test techniques can be established. Conventional test techniques,such as functional tests or scan path tests, are often carried out at low speed. Had these low speed tests been carried out on the FIR filter, the circuits would have incorrectly passed their test. Furthermore the defects would have been extremely difficult to diagnose. A further advantage of the Autonomous Built In Self Test on the FIR filter is that speed parameterisation of the circuit can occur. The FIR filter was specified to operate at 10 MHz. The majority of the circuits operated at this speed over the first four test phases. The clock speed could then be increased until the first four phases of these circuits began to fail. Some circuits began to fail at 13 MHz, whilst other circuits went on to operate at 17 MHz. It is therefore possible to classify these circuits by operating frequencies, all from the same production batch.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A case study in full custom design
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: Sets out to describe a top down design methodology. In reality a top down/bottom up approach is used in full-custom design. Silicon area as a function of cost against a system approach gives this design philosophy. The various objectives set forth dictate a structured approach to design which results in a regular data and control paths, localised communication and extensive concurrency.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A test methodology for VLSI circuits
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: Presents a brief overview of work on testing currently being carried out under the Alvey CAD042 research initiative at Oxford University. A test methodology is being evolved to exploit the hierarchical properties of circuit designs when generating test patterns. The goal of the research is to define a method by which pre-computed test vectors for modules may be combined to form a complete test set for the circuit as a whole. The work is in an early stage of development but initial results, with circuit examples provided by industrial partners in the CAD042 group, have been promising.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: Historically OEMs have generally been reluctant to consider the advantages of incorporation of ASIC devices into their products because of their perception that ASIC technology is risky, expensive and requires special skills and high volumes. Over the last two years all of those 'excuses' have been proven unfounded, but still that perception exists in the market place. The emerging factors that are leading designers down the ASIC road are summarised.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Triple Technology ASICs offer system integration opportunities
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: Sierra Semiconductor Corporation was established in 1983 to serve the market for ASICs requiring its unique Triple Technology. This process technology allows the inclusion of Analogue, Digital and EEPROM on a single device. A library of over 300 cells has been developed for the 2 micron CMOS process including a 34 MHz phase locked loop and an 8-bit microcontroller core, based on National Semiconductor's COP800. The author describes the development of a chip that combined the elements of Analogue, Digital, EEPROM and Microprocessor circuitry in a single device.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A CAL package to link semiconductor process engineering and ECAD
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: Chip design is moving away from simple gate array implementation, in which device parameters and performance are pre-determined, towards semi- or full-custom implementation. Semiconductor processing is the basis of IC design, and it is important that engineers be educated in the properties of their raw materials. The trend towards more fully customised designs puts a premium on accurate knowledge of design parameters and of the origin of design rules. The authors have assembled a package of public domain programs for process simulation and device parameter extraction with graphical output.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: An overview of the ELLA system is given. A major product strategy, to make ELLA more suitable for the design of whole systems, is discussed, and progress with that strategy is explained. Details are given of the algorithmic extensions to ELLA, a new attribute system and a new graphical user interface; all major component parts of the strategy described are available this year.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Custom VLSI Design and Test
abstract: Describes the early stages of the Alvey CAD012 project 'Application Specific Concurrent Testability' (ASCOT), a collaborative venture between the universities of Bath and Hull, Imperial College, London and Silicon Microsystems plc. The main aim of the work at Hull is to develop techniques which would allow circuit testability to be assessed at any point during the design procedure. It rapidly became evident that existing testability measures were very limited in scope and that far more parameters needed to be considered in order to give a realistic picture of testing difficulty. The paper describes the testing problem and then discusses testability parameters of importance before concluding with a brief survey of the current state of the project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
